title: Expected value, variance, Chebyshev
summary: Random variables, their distributions and expected values; linearity of expectation and the indicator method; independence of random variables; variance, Bienaymé’s formula and the binomial mean and variance; and Chebyshev’s inequality. Expect “expected number of …” questions solved with indicators and a variance-plus-Chebyshev computation.

blocks.text: A random variable is a rule that turns each outcome into a number, so you can ask about averages and spreads.
A random variable is a function X : S → ℝ from the sample space to the real numbers. It is neither random nor a variable: it is a fixed function, and the randomness is in which outcome happens.

The distribution of X is the list of pairs (r, p(X = r)) over all values r of X. Here p(X = r) is the probability of the event {s ∈ S : X(s) = r}: list those outcomes and add their probabilities. The probabilities add to 1.

blocks.title: Distribution of the number of heads
blocks.prompt: Flip two fair coins; X = number of heads. Find the distribution of X.
steps: Outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, each 1/4, with X = 2, 1, 1, 0.

blocks.title: Distribution of a dice difference
blocks.prompt: Roll two fair dice; Y = first − second. Find p(Y = −5), p(Y = 0), p(Y = 3) and the whole distribution.
steps: In general p(Y = r) = (6 − |r|)/36 for r = −5, …, 5.

blocks.title: Distribution without replacement
blocks.prompt: An urn has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Draw 2 without replacement; X = number of red balls drawn. Find the distribution of X.
steps: All C(5, 2) = 10 pairs are equally likely.
X = 0: both blue, C(2, 2) = 1 pair, so 1/10.

blocks.text: E(X) = Σ<sub>s∈S</sub> p(s) X(s) = Σ<sub>r</sub> r · p(X = r). The first sum runs over outcomes; the second groups outcomes by value. It is the weighted average of X, the long-run average over many repetitions.

blocks.title: Expected value from the definition
items: List every value r of X.
Find p(X = r) for each (they must add to 1).
Multiply each value by its probability and add.

blocks.title: Expected value by definition
blocks.prompt: Find E(X) for (a) X = heads in two fair coins, (b) one fair die, (c) the urn variable above, and (d) a game that pays 10 dollars with probability 1/5 and costs 2 dollars otherwise.
steps: (b) (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 7/2. The die can never show 3.5: an expected value is an average, not a likely outcome.

blocks.text: Don’t just average the possible values. A coin with p(H) = 0.9 flipped twice has E(heads) = 1.8, not (0 + 1 + 2)/3 = 1.

blocks.name: Linearity of expectation
blocks.text: For any random variables on the same sample space and constants a, b: E(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ) = E(X₁) + ⋯ + E(Xₙ) and E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b. No independence is needed.

proof.text: E(X₁ + X₂) = Σ p(s)(X₁(s) + X₂(s)) = Σ p(s)X₁(s) + Σ p(s)X₂(s) = E(X₁) + E(X₂). Nothing in this algebra uses any relation between X₁ and X₂.
E(aX + b) = Σ p(s)(aX(s) + b) = aΣ p(s)X(s) + bΣ p(s) = aE(X) + b, since the probabilities add to 1. Induct for n terms.

blocks.title: Linearity in one line
blocks.prompt: Find E(first die − second die) and the expected sum of three fair dice.
steps: E(Y₁ − Y₂) = E(Y₁) − E(Y₂) = 7/2 − 7/2 = 0 (compare the long sum over the distribution, where r and −r cancel).
Three dice: 7/2 + 7/2 + 7/2 = 21/2, with no need to list 216 outcomes.

blocks.text: I<sub>A</sub> = 1 if event A happens and 0 otherwise. E(I<sub>A</sub>) = 1 · p(A) + 0 · (1 − p(A)) = p(A).

blocks.title: Expected number of ____ (indicator method)
items: Name the count: X = number of ____.
Write X = I₁ + ⋯ + Iₙ, one indicator per thing that could happen.
Find p(each thing happens); often they are all equal by symmetry.
E(X) = p₁ + ⋯ + pₙ. The indicators may be dependent; linearity does not care.

blocks.title: Binomial mean by indicators
blocks.prompt: n independent trials, each a success with probability p. Find E(number of successes). Then: expected sixes in 12 die rolls; expected heads in 100 flips of a coin with p(H) = 0.3.
steps: Iₖ = 1 if trial k succeeds; E(Iₖ) = p.
X = I₁ + ⋯ + Iₙ, so E(X) = np.

blocks.title: Fixed points of a random permutation
blocks.prompt: n people check hats, and the hats are handed back in a uniformly random order. Find the expected number of people who get their own hat.
steps: Iᵢ = 1 if person i gets their own hat.
E = n · 1/n = 1, for every n, even though the Iᵢ are dependent.

blocks.title: Records
blocks.prompt: n people with different scores arrive in a uniformly random order. A record is a score higher than all earlier ones. Find the expected number of records, and evaluate for n = 4 and n = 100.
steps: Iₖ = 1 if the k-th score is a record, i.e. the largest of the first k.
By symmetry each of the first k scores is equally likely to be the largest: p = 1/k.
n = 4: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 25/12 ≈ 2.08. n = 100: H₁₀₀ ≈ 5.19. Records get rare, since Hₙ grows like ln n.

blocks.text: Doubling after each loss (the martingale) cannot beat a bet with negative expected value: every single bet at roulette has expected value 0.48 − 0.52 = −0.04 dollars per dollar, so by linearity the sum loses on average. The rare long losing streak (10 losses in a row costs 1023 dollars) pays for all the small wins.
X and Y are independent if p(X = r₁ and Y = r₂) = p(X = r₁) p(Y = r₂) for every pair of values r₁, r₂. One failing pair shows they are not independent.

blocks.title: Checking independence of random variables
blocks.prompt: Two fair coins; X = number of heads, Y = number of tails. Are X and Y independent? Are the two dice values of a pair of dice independent?
steps: p(X = 1 and Y = 1) = p({HT, TH}) = 1/2, but (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4. Not independent (X determines Y = 2 − X).
Dice: p(X₁ = a, X₂ = b) = 1/36 = (1/6)(1/6) for every a, b. Independent.
blocks.answer: Heads/tails: not independent; two dice: independent

blocks.name: Expectation of a product
blocks.text: If X and Y are independent, E(XY) = E(X) E(Y).

proof.text: E(XY) = Σ<sub>r₁,r₂</sub> r₁r₂ p(X = r₁, Y = r₂) = Σ<sub>r₁,r₂</sub> r₁r₂ p(X = r₁) p(Y = r₂) (independence, the only place it is used).
The double sum factors: (Σ r₁ p(X = r₁))(Σ r₂ p(Y = r₂)) = E(X)E(Y).

blocks.title: E(XY) with and without independence
blocks.prompt: Two dice: find E(X₁X₂). Two coins: compare E(XY) with E(X)E(Y) for X = heads, Y = tails.
steps: Coins: XY = 0 for HH and TT, and XY = 1 for HT and TH, so E(XY) = 1/2.
E(X)E(Y) = 1 · 1 = 1 ≠ 1/2: the product rule fails without independence.

blocks.text: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) does not prove independence. Sum and difference of two dice satisfy it but are dependent.
V(X) = Σ<sub>s</sub> (X(s) − E(X))² p(s) = E((X − E(X))²), the average squared distance from the mean. σ(X) = √V(X) has the same units as X. V(X) ≥ 0, with equality only if X is constant.

blocks.name: Shortcut formula
blocks.text: V(X) = E(X²) − E(X)².

proof.text: Let μ = E(X). Then (X − μ)² = X² − 2μX + μ². By linearity, E((X − μ)²) = E(X²) − 2μE(X) + μ² = E(X²) − 2μ² + μ² = E(X²) − μ².

blocks.name: Scaling and shifting
blocks.text: V(aX + b) = a² V(X).

proof.text: aX + b − E(aX + b) = a(X − E(X)), and squaring gives a factor a².

blocks.title: Variance by definition and by the shortcut
blocks.prompt: Find V(X) for X = heads in two coins (definition), for one fair die (shortcut), and for the urn variable (3 red, 2 blue, draw 2).
steps: Coins: E(X) = 1. Squared distances: TT → 1, HT/TH → 0, HH → 1. V = 1/4 · 1 + 1/2 · 0 + 1/4 · 1 = 1/2.

blocks.text: E(X²) is not E(X)². For a die, 91/6 ≈ 15.17 vs 49/4 = 12.25; their difference is the variance.

lesson.title: Variance of sums: Bienaymé and the binomial

blocks.name: Bienaymé’s formula
blocks.text: If X₁, …, Xₙ are pairwise independent, V(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ) = V(X₁) + ⋯ + V(Xₙ).

proof.text: Two variables: V(X + Y) = E((X + Y)²) − (E(X) + E(Y))² = [E(X²) + 2E(XY) + E(Y²)] − [E(X)² + 2E(X)E(Y) + E(Y)²].
Independence gives E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross terms cancel, leaving (E(X²) − E(X)²) + (E(Y²) − E(Y)²) = V(X) + V(Y). For n variables the cross terms are pairs, so pairwise independence is enough.

blocks.name: Binomial mean and variance
blocks.text: If X counts successes in n independent trials with success probability p, then E(X) = np and V(X) = np(1 − p).

proof.text: X = I₁ + ⋯ + Iₙ. Since Iₖ² = Iₖ, E(Iₖ²) = p and V(Iₖ) = p − p² = p(1 − p).
The trials are independent, so by Bienaymé V(X) = np(1 − p); by linearity E(X) = np.

blocks.title: Using Bienaymé
blocks.prompt: Find the variance of the sum of two fair dice, and the mean, variance and standard deviation of the number of heads in 100 flips with p(H) = 0.3.

blocks.text: Variances only add under independence. Heads + tails of two coins is always 2, so V(X + Y) = 0, while V(X) + V(Y) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. Likewise V(X + X) = 4V(X), not 2V(X).
If the variance is small, X cannot often be far from its mean. Chebyshev turns that into a number using only E(X) and V(X).

blocks.name: Chebyshev’s inequality
blocks.text: For any random variable X and any r > 0, p(|X − E(X)| ≥ r) ≤ V(X)/r².

proof.text: Let A = {s : |X(s) − E(X)| ≥ r}. Start from the definition of variance:
V(X) = Σ<sub>all s</sub> (X(s) − E(X))² p(s) ≥ Σ<sub>s∈A</sub> (X(s) − E(X))² p(s) ≥ Σ<sub>s∈A</sub> r² p(s) = r² p(A)
The first ≥ drops the nonnegative terms outside A; the second uses (X(s) − E(X))² ≥ r² on A. Divide by r².

blocks.title: Chebyshev problems
items: Find E(X) and V(X) (linearity, Bienaymé, binomial formulas).
Rewrite the event as “at least r away from the mean” and read off r.
The answer is the bound V(X)/r², an upper bound and not the exact probability.

blocks.title: Bound vs exact: 100 coins
blocks.prompt: X = heads in 100 fair flips. Bound p(|X − 50| ≥ 10) with Chebyshev and compare with the exact value.
steps: The exact binomial value is about 0.057, far below 1/4: Chebyshev is always valid but usually loose.

blocks.title: Bound vs exact: one die
blocks.prompt: Roll one fair die. Use Chebyshev to bound p(the roll is 1 or 6), and compare.
steps: Rolling 1 or 6 means being exactly 5/2 from the mean, so r = 5/2.
True value: 2/6 = 1/3 ≤ 7/15, as it must be.

blocks.title: Chebyshev for a binomial count
blocks.prompt: A fair die is rolled 600 times; X = number of sixes. Bound p(|X − 100| ≥ 20).

blocks.title: How many trials?
blocks.prompt: n fair coins; X = heads. Show p(|X − n/2| ≥ √n) ≤ 1/4 for every n.

blocks.text: Divide by r², and use the variance, not σ. Never present the bound as the exact probability.

cards.front: What is a random variable?

back.text: X : S → ℝ
Meaning. A random variable X is a rule that gives every outcome s in the sample space S a number X(s). It turns outcomes (like “HT”) into numbers you can average.
The name is misleading: X is not random and not a variable. It’s a fixed function. The randomness is only in which outcome happens.
Example. Flip two fair coins; X = number of heads. X(HH) = 2, X(HT) = 1, X(TH) = 1, X(TT) = 0.

cards.front: What does p(X = r) mean, and how do you compute it?

back.text: Meaning. p(X = r) is the probability of the event “X equals r”: the set of all outcomes s with X(s) = r.
How.

items: List every outcome that gives X the value r.
Add up their probabilities.

back.text: Example. Two fair coins, X = heads. Each outcome has probability 1/4. p(X = 2) = 1/4 (just HH). p(X = 1) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HT and TH). p(X = 0) = 1/4. The three add to 1, a good check.

cards.front: Roll two fair dice; Y = first number − second number. Find p(Y = −5), p(Y = 0) and p(Y = 3).

back.text: There are 36 equally likely ordered outcomes, each 1/36.
Order matters: (4,1) and (1,4) are different outcomes, and (1,4) gives −3, not 3.

cards.front: What is the expected value E(X), and what does it mean?

back.text: E(X) = Σ over outcomes s of p(s)·X(s)
= Σ over values r of r · p(X = r)
Meaning. The weighted average of X: each value counts in proportion to how likely it is. Repeat the experiment many times and the average of X settles near E(X).
The two formulas agree: the second just groups together outcomes that give the same value. Use whichever is easier.
How.

items: List the possible values r of X.
Find p(X = r) for each (they must add to 1).
Multiply each value by its probability and add.

cards.front: Two fair coins, X = number of heads. Find E(X) directly.

back.text: E(X) = 1. It makes sense: two coins, each heads half the time, so one head on average.

cards.front: What is E(X) for one roll of a fair die? Can the die ever show E(X)?

back.text: E(X) = 7/2 = 3.5. Each face has probability 1/6.
No: 3.5 is not a face. The expected value is an average, not a likely outcome, and it doesn’t have to be a possible value.

cards.front: Why can’t you just average the possible values of X to get E(X)?

back.text: Because values aren’t equally likely in general. You must weight each value by its probability.
A biased coin has p(H) = 0.9. Flip it twice; X = heads. The values 0, 1, 2 average to 1, but E(X) = 0·0.01 + 1·0.18 + 2·0.81 = 1.8.
For fair coins the plain average happens to give the right answer. Don’t rely on that.

cards.front: A game: win 10 dollars with probability 1/5, lose 2 dollars otherwise. Expected winnings?

back.text: $0.40 per game. Losses are just negative values; “otherwise” has probability 1 − 1/5 = 4/5.

cards.front: State linearity of expectation.

back.text: E(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ) = E(X₁) + ⋯ + E(Xₙ)
E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b
Meaning. The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values. Constants pull out, and shifts just shift the average.
This works always: the Xᵢ do not need to be independent.

cards.front: Why is linearity of expectation true?

back.text: Proof. Write E as a sum over outcomes and split it:
E(X₁ + X₂) = Σ p(s)(X₁(s) + X₂(s))
= Σ p(s)X₁(s) + Σ p(s)X₂(s) = E(X₁) + E(X₂)
Nothing in that algebra cares whether X₁ and X₂ are related, so no independence is needed.
For aX + b: Σ p(s)(aX(s) + b) = a·Σ p(s)X(s) + b·Σ p(s) = aE(X) + b, since the probabilities add to 1.

cards.front: Use linearity to find E(first die − second die).

items: Let Y₁ = first die, Y₂ = second die. Then Y = Y₁ − Y₂.

back.text: Same answer as the long way, in one line. (The minus sign is linearity with a = −1.)

cards.front: Expected sum of three fair dice?

back.text: 21/2 = 10.5. Listing all 6³ = 216 outcomes would take forever; linearity takes one line.

cards.front: What is an indicator random variable, and what is its expected value?

back.text: Xₖ = 1 if event k happens, 0 if not ⟹ E(Xₖ) = p(event k)
Why it matters. Any count is a sum of indicators: “number of heads” = (1 if flip 1 is H) + (1 if flip 2 is H) + ⋯. So by linearity, the expected count = the sum of the probabilities.

cards.front: What is the recipe for “expected number of ____” problems?

back.text: The indicator trick.

items: Name the count: X = number of ____.
Write X = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ, one indicator for each thing that could happen.
Find p(each thing happens). Often they’re all equal by symmetry.
Add: E(X) = p₁ + ⋯ + pₙ.

back.text: You never need the distribution of X itself.
The indicators can depend on each other. Don’t stop to check independence; linearity doesn’t need it.

cards.front: n independent trials, each a success with probability p. Expected number of successes? Why?

back.text: E(X) = np
Why.

items: Xₖ = 1 if trial k succeeds, else 0. So X = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ.
By linearity, E(X) = p + p + ⋯ + p (n times) = np.

back.text: Example. 100 coins with a 3/10 chance of heads: E = 100 · 0.3 = 30 heads.

cards.front: Roll a fair die 12 times. Expected number of sixes? And 10 flips of a coin with p(H) = 0.2: expected heads?

back.text: Both are Bernoulli trials, so E = np.

cards.front: 100 people with different scores appear in a random order. A “record” is a score higher than all before it. Expected number of records?

back.text: How.

items: Xₖ = 1 if the k-th score is a record. X = X₁ + ⋯ + X₁₀₀.
The k-th score is a record exactly when it’s the largest of the first k. Each of those k scores is equally likely to be the largest, so p = 1/k.
Add: E(X) = Σ 1/k = H₁₀₀ ≈ 5.19.

back.text: Hₙ (the harmonic number) grows like ln n, so records get rarer and rarer.

cards.front: The “martingale”: bet 1 dollar at roulette, double after every loss, stop at the first win. Why does each round end 1 dollar ahead?

back.text: If you lose k − 1 times and then win, you lost 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 2ᵏ⁻² and won 2ᵏ⁻¹.
So when the win comes, the profit is exactly $1.

cards.front: Why doesn’t the martingale guarantee a profit? (Roulette: win 48%, lose 52%.)

items: Every bet has expected value 0.48 − 0.52 = −$0.04 per dollar. By linearity, a sum of losing bets has negative expected value. No strategy fixes that.
The rare disaster is huge: 10 losses in a row (probability 0.52¹⁰ ≈ 0.0014) costs 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 512 = $1023, and you may not have money for the next bet.
Play enough rounds and that streak becomes likely, wiping out all the $1 wins.

cards.front: When are random variables X and Y independent?

back.text: p(X = r₁ and Y = r₂) = p(X = r₁) · p(Y = r₂) for all r₁, r₂
Meaning. Knowing the value of X tells you nothing about Y. Equivalently, every event “X = r₁” is independent of every event “Y = r₂”.
How to show NOT independent. Find one pair r₁, r₂ where the equation fails.
Example. Two dice, X = first, Y = second: p(X = r₁, Y = r₂) = 1/36 = (1/6)(1/6) for every pair, so they’re independent.

cards.front: Two fair coins, X = number of heads, Y = number of tails. Show X and Y are not independent.

items: But (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 ≠ 1/2. Not independent.

back.text: Makes sense: X + Y = 2 always, so knowing X tells you Y exactly.

cards.front: When is E(XY) = E(X)·E(Y)? Why?

back.text: X, Y independent ⟹ E(XY) = E(X)E(Y)
Why.

items: E(XY) = Σ over r₁, r₂ of r₁r₂ · p(X = r₁ and Y = r₂).
Independence splits the probability: p(X = r₁)·p(Y = r₂). This is the only step that uses independence.
The double sum factors: (Σ r₁ p(X = r₁))·(Σ r₂ p(Y = r₂)) = E(X)E(Y).

back.text: Linearity works for sums always; this product rule needs independence.

cards.front: Show E(XY) ≠ E(X)E(Y) for X = heads, Y = tails of two fair coins.

back.text: ½ ≠ 1, which is fine: X and Y aren’t independent.

cards.front: What are variance and standard deviation, and what do they measure?

back.text: V(X) = Σ over s of (X(s) − E(X))² · p(s)
σ(X) = √V(X)
Meaning. E(X) is the center. Variance measures spread: the average squared distance from E(X). Squaring makes all distances positive and punishes big ones more.
σ, the standard deviation, undoes the square, so it’s in the same units as X: roughly “how far from the mean X typically lands”.
V(X) ≥ 0 always, and V(X) = 0 only if X is constant.

cards.front: Two fair coins, X = heads. Find V(X) from the definition.

items: Squared distances: TT → (0 − 1)² = 1; HT, TH → 0; HH → (2 − 1)² = 1.

cards.front: What is the shortcut formula for variance, and why does it hold?

back.text: V(X) = E(X²) − E(X)²
“Mean of the square minus square of the mean.”
Why.

items: Write μ = E(X). Expand: (X − μ)² = X² − 2μX + μ².
Take E using linearity: E(X²) − 2μE(X) + μ² = E(X²) − 2μ² + μ².
= E(X²) − μ².

back.text: How. Compute E(X), then E(X²) = Σ r²·p(X = r) (square the values, keep the probabilities), then subtract.

cards.front: Find the variance of one roll of a fair die.

back.text: E(X²) is not E(X)²: 91/6 ≈ 15.17 vs. 49/4 = 12.25. Their difference is exactly the variance.

cards.front: What is V(aX + b)?

back.text: V(aX + b) = a² · V(X)
Why. Adding b shifts every value and the mean by b, so distances from the mean don’t change. Multiplying by a multiplies every distance by a, so squared distances by a².

cards.front: X is 0 or 10, each with probability ½. Find V(X) and σ(X).

back.text: Every value is exactly 5 from the mean, which matches σ = 5.

cards.front: State Bienaymé’s formula.

back.text: X₁, …, Xₙ independent ⟹ V(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ) = V(X₁) + ⋯ + V(Xₙ)
Meaning. For independent variables, variances add, just like expectations. Unlike linearity, this needs independence.

cards.front: Why are variances additive for two independent variables?

items: V(X₁ + X₂) = E((X₁ + X₂)²) − (E(X₁) + E(X₂))².
Expand: E(X₁²) + 2E(X₁X₂) + E(X₂²) − [E(X₁)² + 2E(X₁)E(X₂) + E(X₂)²].
Independence gives E(X₁X₂) = E(X₁)E(X₂), so the two cross terms cancel.
Left: [E(X₁²) − E(X₁)²] + [E(X₂²) − E(X₂)²] = V(X₁) + V(X₂).

back.text: Without independence the cross terms stay, and the formula can fail.

cards.front: Variance of the sum of two fair dice?

back.text: The dice are independent, and each has variance 35/12.

cards.front: Show variances don’t add without independence (X = heads, Y = tails, two coins).

back.text: X + Y = 2 always, so V(X + Y) = 0.
But V(X) + V(Y) = ½ + ½ = 1.
Before adding variances, check independence. (Adding expectations never needs it.)

cards.front: Variance of the number of successes in n independent trials with success probability p? Why?

back.text: V(X) = np(1 − p)
Why.

items: Indicators: X = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ, Xₖ = 1 on success.
Xₖ is 0 or 1, so Xₖ² = Xₖ and E(Xₖ²) = p.
V(Xₖ) = E(Xₖ²) − E(Xₖ)² = p − p² = p(1 − p).
The trials are independent, so by Bienaymé, V(X) = n·p(1 − p).

cards.front: 100 coins with p(H) = 0.3: variance and standard deviation of heads? And 10 flips with p = 0.2?
State Chebyshev’s inequality and say what it’s for.

back.text: p( |X − E(X)| ≥ r ) ≤ V(X) / r²
Meaning. For any random variable and any r > 0: the chance X lands at least r away from its mean is at most variance over r².
Small variance means X rarely strays far. It needs only E(X) and V(X), not the whole distribution.
It gives an upper bound (≤), not the exact probability. Use V, not σ, and square r.

cards.front: Why is Chebyshev’s inequality true?

back.text: Let A = the outcomes where |X(s) − E(X)| ≥ r.

items: V(X) = Σ over all s of (X(s) − E(X))² p(s).
Drop the outcomes outside A. Every term is ≥ 0, so the sum can only shrink: V(X) ≥ Σ over s in A.
Inside A, each (X(s) − E(X))² ≥ r², so V(X) ≥ Σ over s in A of r² p(s) = r²·p(A).
Divide by r²: p(A) ≤ V(X)/r².

cards.front: What is the recipe for a Chebyshev problem?

items: Find E(X) and V(X), usually with indicators, np and np(1 − p).
Rewrite the event as “at least r away from the mean” to read off r.
Answer: probability ≤ V(X)/r².

back.text: “At most 40 or at least 60 heads out of 100” = “at least 10 away from 50”, so r = 10.

cards.front: Why does linearity of expectation not need independence, while adding variances does?

back.text: E(X + Y) = Σ p(s)(X(s) + Y(s)) splits for any X, Y. V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y) + 2(E(XY) − E(X)E(Y)), and the cross term vanishes only when E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), e.g. under independence.

cards.front: Expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of n items?

back.text: Indicators Iᵢ for “i is fixed”, each with probability 1/n. Its variance is also 1, but you cannot get that from Bienaymé: the Iᵢ are dependent.

prompt.text: A fair coin is flipped n times. A run is a maximal block of equal outcomes (HHTHH has 3 runs). Find the expected number of runs.

solution.text: Runs = 1 + (number of positions i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1, where flip i ≠ flip i + 1). Let Ii indicate a change at position i, so P(Ii = 1) = 1/2. By linearity, E = 1 + (n − 1)/2 = (n + 1)/2. For n = 10 that is 5.5.
Tests: writing a messy count as a constant plus a sum of indicators. Common mistake: trying to find the full distribution of the number of runs. Linearity doesn’t need it.

prompt.text: (a) A die is rolled 6 times. Find the expected number of distinct values seen. (b) Find the expected number of inversions (pairs i < j with π(i) > π(j)) in a uniformly random permutation of {1..n}.

solution.text: (a) For each face v, let Iv = 1 if v appears. P(Iv = 1) = 1 − (5/6)⁶. So E = 6(1 − (5/6)⁶) = 31031/7776 ≈ 3.99.
(b) One indicator for each of the C(n,2) pairs of positions. By symmetry, the pair is inverted with probability 1/2. E = n(n − 1)/4.

Tests: choosing what to index the indicators by (faces, not rolls; pairs, not elements). Common mistake: in (a), the indicators are dependent, but linearity doesn’t care. Don’t multiply probabilities.

prompt.text: Find the expected number of rolls of a fair die needed to see all six faces.

solution.text: Split the wait into stages. After i − 1 distinct faces have been seen, each roll shows a new face with probability (7 − i)/6. The stage length is geometric, with mean 6/(7 − i). By linearity:
Tests: the geometric mean 1/p, plus splitting into stages. Common mistake: answering 6·6 = 36, or 6.

hard.title: Variance of the number of fixed points

prompt.text: Let X be the number of fixed points of a uniformly random permutation of {1..n} (n ≥ 2). Find V(X). Why can’t you use Bienaymé’s formula?

hard.answer: V(X) = 2 − 1² = 1; Bienaymé fails because the indicators are dependent.

solution.text: X = Σ I<sub>i</sub> with P(I<sub>i</sub> = 1) = 1/n, so E[X] = 1.

E[X²] = Σ<sub>i</sub> E[I<sub>i</sub>²] + Σ<sub>i≠j</sub> E[I<sub>i</sub>I<sub>j</sub>] = n·(1/n) + n(n − 1)·1/(n(n − 1)) = 2. Here I<sub>i</sub>² = I<sub>i</sub>, and both i and j are fixed with probability (n − 2)!/n!.
Answer: V(X) = 2 − 1² = 1.

The I<sub>i</sub> are not independent (if n − 1 points are fixed, so is the last one), so the variance of the sum is not the sum of the variances. That would give n·(1/n)(1 − 1/n) = 1 − 1/n, which is wrong.
Tests: expanding E[X²] over pairs of indicators. Common mistake: applying Bienaymé to dependent indicators.

hard.title: Uncorrelated but dependent

prompt.text: Roll two dice, X<sub>1</sub> and X<sub>2</sub>.

items: (a) Show that S = X<sub>1</sub> + X<sub>2</sub> and D = X<sub>1</sub> − X<sub>2</sub> satisfy E[SD] = E[S]E[D], yet are not independent.
(b) Are X<sub>1</sub> and Y = max(X<sub>1</sub>, X<sub>2</sub>) independent?
(c) Give a random variable X for which V(X + X) ≠ V(X) + V(X).

hard.answer: (a) E[SD] = 0 = E[S]E[D] but P(S=2, D=0) = 1/36 ≠ 1/216 (b) not independent (c) V(X + X) = 4V(X) ≠ 2V(X) for any nonconstant X

solution.text: (a) E[SD] = E[X<sub>1</sub>²] − E[X<sub>2</sub>²] = 0 and E[D] = 0, so E[SD] = 0 = E[S]E[D]. But P(S = 2, D = 0) = P((1,1)) = 1/36, while P(S = 2)P(D = 0) = (1/36)(1/6). Not independent.
(c) Take any X with V(X) > 0, for example one die. Then V(2X) = 4V(X) ≠ 2V(X). Bienaymé needs independence, and X is not independent of itself.
Tests: independence means every pair of values multiplies. A product rule for expectations is not enough. Common mistake: treating “E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]” as a proof of independence.

hard.title: Chebyshev sample size for coin flips

prompt.text: How many flips n of a fair coin does Chebyshev’s inequality say are enough to guarantee that the fraction of heads is within 0.05 of 1/2 with probability at least 0.99?

solution.text: Let X be the number of heads. Then V(X) = n/4 (Bienaymé, since the flips are independent), so V(X/n) = 1/(4n). Chebyshev: P(|X/n − 1/2| ≥ 0.05) ≤ (1/(4n))/0.05² = 100/n.
Tests: scaling the variance: V(X/n) = V(X)/n². Common mistake: dividing by n instead of n², or using the standard deviation in place of the variance.

prompt.text: A standard deck is shuffled and cards are turned over one at a time until the first ace appears. What is the expected number of cards turned over, including the ace?

solution.text: For each of the 48 non-aces c, let I<sub>c</sub> = 1 if c comes before all four aces. Among c and the 4 aces, each of the 5 is equally likely to come first, so P(I<sub>c</sub> = 1) = 1/5.
Number of cards turned = 1 (the first ace) + Σ Ic, so E = 1 + 48/5 = 53/5 = 10.6.

Tests: using an indicator for each object that comes before the event. Common mistake: treating the draws as independent with probability 4/52 each (that gives 13). These draws are without replacement.

prompt.text: Find the expected number of flips of a fair coin until HH first appears, and until HT first appears. Explain why they are different.

solution.text: HH. Let E be the expected number of flips from the start, and EH the expected number still needed when the last flip was H. Then:
E = 1 + ½E<sub>H</sub> + ½E
E<sub>H</sub> = 1 + ½·0 + ½E
The first equation gives E = 2 + EH. Substituting into the second, EH = 1 + 1 + EH/2, so EH = 4 and E = 6.
HT. Wait for the first H (expected 2 flips). After that, extra H’s don’t lose anything, so wait for a T (expected 2 more). E = 4.
Why they differ. While building HH, a T after an H sends you back to the start. While building HT, a wrong flip (another H) leaves you exactly where you were. Failure is cheaper for HT.
Tests: setting up linear equations by conditioning on the first flip. Common mistake: “every 2-flip pattern has probability 1/4, so the expected wait is 4 for both”.

hard.title: Die rolls, Chebyshev and overlapping patterns

prompt.text: (a) A fair die is rolled 90 times. Let X be the number of rolls showing 1 or 2. Find E(X) and V(X), and use Chebyshev’s inequality to bound P(|X − 30| ≥ 10).
(b) A fair coin is flipped 12 times. Find the expected number of times the pattern HTH appears in three consecutive flips (overlaps count: HTHTH contains it twice).
(c) Let Ij be the indicator that HTH starts at flip j. Are I1 and I2 independent? Are I1 and I3? Does your answer affect part (b)?

hard.answer: (a) E = 30, V = 20, P(|X − 30| ≥ 10) ≤ 1/5 (b) 10 · 1/8 = 5/4 (c) I₁, I₂ dependent; I₁, I₃ dependent; (b) unaffected (linearity)

solution.text: (a) X is binomial with n = 90, p = 2/6 = 1/3 (the rolls are independent).
(The true value is about 0.033. Chebyshev is crude but always valid.)
(b) HTH can start at flips 1, 2, …, 10 (it needs 3 flips): 10 positions. Let Ij indicate that flips j, j+1, j+2 read HTH; E(Ij) = (1/2)³ = 1/8. By linearity of expectation:
E(count) = Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>10</sup> E(I<sub>j</sub>) = 10 · 1/8 = 5/4
(c) I1 = I2 = 1 would need flip 2 to be T (for I1) and H (for I2). Impossible, so P(I1 = I2 = 1) = 0 ≠ (1/8)² = 1/64. Not independent.
I1 = I3 = 1 means flips 1–5 read HTHTH: probability 1/32 ≠ 1/64. Not independent either (they share flip 3).
No effect on (b): linearity of expectation holds for any random variables, independent or not. (Independence would matter for the variance.)
Recognizing a binomial, Chebyshev’s inequality, indicator variables with linearity, and knowing linearity needs no independence.
Using 12 positions instead of 10 in (b). Believing E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) requires independence; it’s V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y) that does.
